meta.description: Shaw called it a flat lie in his own hand and Churchill agreed. The earliest printing anyone has found is from 1946, about Noel Coward and Randolph Churchill.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Here are Two Tickets for the Opening of My Play. Bring a Friend—If You Have One'?
meta.ogDescription: Both men denied it in writing in 1949, and the letters survive. The earliest printed version anyone has found, from 1946, is about two entirely different people.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — a joke he called “a flat lie”
answer.authorDates: Earliest print 19 September 1946 · told then of Noël Coward and Randolph Churchill
answer.sourceLine: There is no letter, no playbill and no contemporary source — and both supposed correspondents denied it in writing. The earliest printing anyone has found is Walter Winchell’s column of September 1946, where the joke is told of Noël Coward and Randolph Churchill; Shaw and Winston Churchill’s names are attached to it only in January 1948.

source.heading: The earliest Shaw–Churchill telling

docMeta.dd: Fabricated — denied in writing by both men
Bob Considine, International News Service, January 1948

source.excerpt: George Bernard Shaw sent Winston Churchill a couple of seats for the opening night of one of his plays, some time ago… Shaw enclosed a little note with the tickets. It read, “Here are two tickets for the opening of my new play. Keep one for yourself and bring along a friend—if you can find one.” Churchill returned the tickets with a nice little note, too. “I’m sorry that a previous engagement precludes my attending your opening night,” he said. “I shall be happy to come the second night—if there is one.”
trail: 19 September 1946 — the earliest printed version Quote Investigator has located ↗ runs in Walter Winchell’s syndicated column, and Shaw is not in it. Randolph Churchill asks Noël Coward for two tickets, receives one, and is told: “Let me know if you really have a friend and I’ll send you the other ticket.” A closely similar Coward-to-Randolph version appears in Arthur Porritt’s More and More of Memories the following year.

January 1948 — Shaw and Winston Churchill’s names appear for the first time, in an International News Service piece by Bob Considine that QI traces to the St. Joseph Gazette of 12 January 1948 ↗. QI observes that the Shaw plays later named as the occasion all opened in the 1910s and 1920s, which makes a first appearance in the 1940s surprising.

15–16 September 1949 — the denials. Asked for permission to print the story, Shaw wrote across the enclosure that it was “not only a flat lie but a political libel”; the next day Churchill’s secretary replied that Churchill “considers Mr. Bernard Shaw is quite right.” Both letters were found in the Churchill Papers by the Churchill Archives Centre’s director ↗, filed at CHUR 2/165/66,68.
Today — the exchange still circulates without a source. Wikiquote keeps it on Shaw’s talk page under ‘Unsourced’ ↗, in a wording different again from the popular one, with no citation offered.
source.excerptNote: This is the oldest known printing that names Shaw and Winston Churchill — a newspaper columnist relaying gossip overheard at a New York City Hall portrait unveiling, not a letter. Note that it does not match the wording that circulates today. The familiar phrase “bring a friend—if you have one” is absent from the earliest tellings of 1946, 1947 and January 1948; it is in print by October 1948 and is fixed in its popular form by Kay Halle’s Irrepressible Churchill (1966), which is the wording Quote Investigator took for its headline.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the wording has no identifiable author. The line is not traceable to any work by Shaw, and the documented early tellings are anonymous newspaper items — and those 1946 and 1948 newspaper texts are post-1930, so their United States status turns on whether the copyright was renewed in its 28th year, which we have not checked. Shaw’s own writings from before 1931 are a separate matter; either way, this sentence is simply not among them.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: The man who denied it
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic & polemicist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1925
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic and political polemicist whose influence on Western theatre ran from the 1880s until his death, and who took the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925. He was a famously combative correspondent, which is precisely why jokes like this one stick to him so easily. It is also why the record is unusually clear here: asked in 1949 whether the ticket exchange could be printed, Shaw wrote across the page in his own hand that it was “not only a flat lie but a political libel.”

copyAttribution: Not George Bernard Shaw. The "two tickets — bring a friend, if you have one" exchange with Winston Churchill is unsupported: Shaw wrote in his own hand, on Derek Tatham's letter of 15 September 1949, that it was "not only a flat lie but a political libel," and Churchill's office agreed the next day (Churchill Papers, CHUR 2/165/66,68, Churchill Archives Centre). The joke's earliest known printing, in Walter Winchell's column of 19 September 1946, tells it of Noël Coward and Randolph Churchill. The wording that follows is the popular form as given in Kay Halle, Irrepressible Churchill (1966), p.116 — not a wording either man wrote. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited, and what the record shows
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely repeated exchanges in English anecdote, and it has been recast repeatedly — the names swapped upward toward fame as it spread. Unusually for a quote of this kind, the record carries a denial in Shaw’s own hand and a same-day confirmation from Churchill’s office.

items.tag: Denied it in his own hand
items.why: On 15 September 1949 the bookseller’s representative Derek Tatham wrote to Shaw asking whether he objected to the story being printed. Shaw scrawled his answer directly on the enclosure: “The above is not only a flat lie but a political libel which may possibly damage me. Publish it at your peril, whether in assertion or contradiction.” The Churchill Project reproduces the note in facsimile ↗.

items.scope: The reply about the second night
items.why: Tatham then approached Churchill. His secretary Elizabeth Gilliatt replied on 16 September 1949: “I am desired by Mr. Churchill…to inform you that he considers Mr. Bernard Shaw is quite right in calling the incident to which you refer ‘a flat lie.’” Both letters sit in the Churchill Papers at CHUR 2/165/66,68 ↗.

In 1946 Coward sends Randolph Churchill, Winston’s son, a single ticket; the 1947 Porritt version already has two, one of them for the friend — if he has a friend. By 1964 a further variant had Coward writing to Winston Churchill instead — a telling the newspaper that printed it expressly labelled apocryphal. Quote Investigator lays out each recasting in order ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No letter, no date and no play has ever been produced. The oldest trace is a 1946 newspaper gag about two different men, and the only primary documents in the case are the two 1949 letters in which Shaw calls the story a flat lie and Churchill’s secretary confirms he agrees — held at the Churchill Archives Centre ↗.

context.heading: Why this one refuses to die
lead: It is a perfect joke, which is exactly the problem. The setup needs no context, the punchline lands twice, and it flatters two men whose public personalities were built on precisely this kind of needling. A story that good does not need a source to travel — and this one travelled for decades without ever acquiring one.

The documentary trail runs backwards from fame rather than forwards from an event. The oldest version, in 1946, pins the gag on Noël Coward and Randolph Churchill — the less famous playwright and the less famous Churchill. Within about two years both roles had been recast with the bigger names, the exchange had grown a second half, and it had begun acquiring specifics it never had at the start. Quote Investigator notes the awkward arithmetic plainly: the Shaw plays later named as the occasion all opened in the 1910s and 1920s, yet the anecdote itself does not appear in print until the 1940s.
context.detailsSummary: The one account that says Shaw told it himself — and how the standard reference work changed its mind
detailsBody: Honesty requires flagging the evidence that cuts the other way. In the 1962 symposium Shaw the Villager and Human Being, assembled by Allan Chappelow, an orthopaedic surgeon named L. W. Plewes — who treated Shaw in 1950, when Shaw was 94 — recalled Shaw himself relating the exchange, and placing it before the first staging of Pygmalion. That is a secondhand recollection of a very old man, published after his death, and it sits directly against Shaw’s own signed denial of a decade earlier; but it is the reason Quote Investigator leaves the case formally open ↗ rather than closing it.

The reference works have moved. Richard Langworth’s Churchill by Himself (2008) included the anecdote, dating it to 1922 and naming the play as Saint Joan. Writing for the Churchill Project in 2020, after Churchill Archives Centre director Allen Packwood surfaced the Tatham correspondence, Langworth called the exchange fictitious ↗ and identified the play at issue in that 1949 correspondence as Buoyant Billions, Shaw’s last full-length play.

Note also that the popular wording is younger than the anecdote. The phrasing that circulates today — “bring a friend—if you have one” — is absent from the earliest tellings, which word the punchline differently each time: “if you really have a friend” in 1946, “if you have a friend” in 1947, “if you can find one” in January 1948. It reaches print in October 1948, in an address by Robert L. Stearns, and settles into its familiar form in Kay Halle’s Irrepressible Churchill (1966), p.116 — the version Quote Investigator took for its headline and the one Wikiquote reproduces.
context.pull: The above is not only a flat lie but a political libel which may possibly damage me. — Shaw, in his own hand

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest printed evidence QI located is a September 1946 Walter Winchell column in which the joke concerns Randolph Churchill and Noël Coward, not Shaw and Winston Churchill; Coward's note reads 'Let me know if you really have a friend and I'll send you the other ticket.'

The first Shaw–Churchill version QI found is a January 1948 International News Service article by Bob Considine (St. Joseph Gazette, 12 January 1948, p.9), reading 'Here are two tickets for the opening of my new play. Keep one for yourself and bring along a friend—if you can find one,' with Churchill's reply 'I shall be happy to come the second night—if there is one.'

QI documents the 1947 Porritt 'More and More of Memories' Coward/Randolph version, the 1962 Chappelow symposium account by surgeon L. W. Plewes (who treated Shaw in 1950 at age 94 and said Shaw placed it before Pygmalion), the 1964 Coward/Winston variant labelled apocryphal by the printing newspaper, and Langworth's 2008 'Churchill by Himself' dating of 1922 with Saint Joan; QI concludes with two unresolved possibilities.

QI notes the Shaw plays named in the various citations opened in the 1910s and 1920s, making the 1940s first printings surprising. The page's own title is 'Quote Origin: Here are Two Tickets for the Opening of My Play. Bring a Friend—If You Have One'; the popular wording is QI's headline, and QI transcribes it from Kay Halle, Irrepressible Churchill (1966), p.116 — 'Am reserving two tickets for you for my premiere. Come and bring a friend—if you have one.' It also appears in QI's October 1948 citation, an address by Robert L. Stearns ('come and bring a friend—if you have one'), while the 1946, 1947 and January 1948 citations word the punchline differently.

Richard Langworth, writing for the Churchill Project (Hillsdale College), calls the exchange fictitious; Allen Packwood, director of the Churchill Archives Centre, found letters in the Churchill Papers (CHUR 2/165/66,68) in which both Shaw and Churchill denied it, and the play in question was Buoyant Billions (1948).

On 15 September 1949 Derek Tatham, representing London booksellers Alfred Wilson, wrote to Shaw; Shaw scrawled in his own hand 'The above is not only a flat lie but a political libel which may possibly damage me. Publish it at your peril, whether in assertion or contradiction.' Churchill's secretary Elizabeth Gilliatt replied on the 16th that Churchill 'considers Mr. Bernard Shaw is quite right in calling the incident to which you refer a flat lie.'

Langworth's own site carries the same account, including the facsimile caption crediting Allen Packwood and Churchill Archives Centre CHUR 2/165, and states there is no other contemporary appearance of the Shaw-Churchill exchange.

This attachment page on the Churchill Project site hosts the ShawTatham image — the facsimile of Shaw's handwritten dismissal, captioned on the parent article as reproduced by kind permission of Allen Packwood, Churchill Archives Centre, CHUR 2/165.

Wikiquote's Talk:George Bernard Shaw page lists the exchange in a section headed 'Unsourced', worded 'Shaw: Am reserving two seats for my show. Come bring a friend - if you have one. / Winston Churchill: Impossible to be present for the first one. Will attend the second — if there is one,' with no citation. The main Wikiquote George Bernard Shaw article carries it separately, under 'Misattributed', in the Kay Halle wording ('Am reserving two tickets for you for my premiere. Come and bring a friend—if you have one.'), citing Irrepressible Churchill (1966) and the QI article.

This is the collection-level catalogue record for The Papers of Sir Winston Churchill (Reference Code GBR/0014/CHAR, CHUR and CHAQ) held at Churchill Archives Centre, comprising the Chartwell Papers (CHAR), Churchill Papers (CHUR) and additional material (CHAQ), with CHUR 2 covering Public and Political: general.

Buoyant Billions is George Bernard Shaw's last full-length play, begun in 1946 and completed in 1948, premiered at the Schauspielhaus Zürich on 21 October 1948 in German translation, with a limited edition published in London in 1949.
George Bernard Shaw lived 26 July 1856 – 2 November 1950, was an Irish playwright, critic, polemicist and political activist, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.
